Moores Lab AI: Applying Agentic AI Across Chip Design

4

Shares

2

EDA startup bets on domain expertise to speed the design process.

September 29th, 2026 -

By: Brendan Heffernan

With the AI boom driving demand for faster semiconductor chip turnarounds, can AI help engineers meet those tighter deadlines?
Startup Moores Lab AI hopes to provide a definitive answer with its end-to-end chip design automation products. Founded last year by chip industry veterans, the company contends that for AI agents to solve chip design problems, they must be designed by people with deep chip design expertise.
“Most of the startups in the same space trying to automate semiconductor flows are all coming from the AI background,” said Shelly Henry, the company’s CEO and co-founder. “We come from the other side. We are semiconductor engineers. We found a new technology in AI and thought about how we can use it to solve our problems. There are two schools of thought there. Their approach is, ‘Let’s make this AI better and better so that it will automatically solve semiconductor problems.’ We are saying, ‘AI is already getting better; let’s build something on top of it.’ That’s where our differentiation is.”
Moores Lab AI’s initial focus is on speeding up verification, debugging, and coverage. “It comes with its own challenges, but what we have built is a technology using AI that will enable you to actually build chips in under six months, from start to finish,” Henry said. “When you’re building a chip, you’re betting on a market two years down the line. It takes a lot of money and effort for those two years to build that chip. We have been trying as a community to reduce this cycle so that it becomes more predictable and less expensive, so that more startups and new endeavors can come into this field.”
The company is also developing a suite of products to automate complex SoC development and verification.
So far, the biggest productivity gains the company’s products have delivered have come through speeding the initial debug phase, Henry said. “We have our system deployed in about 10 different places, and they are using it for different kinds of IP. They’re seeing the biggest jump in initial setup. Usually, it takes about three to four months to get your test plan ready, your test bench ready, and to get all your simulations running, or even the first simulation to run and find the first bug. We consistently see customers jump to the first bug within 48 hours using our platform. All our customers are saying the same thing. That initial thing is compressed right off the bat. Then once they find the first bug, they continuously use our platform to find more and more bugs very quickly.”
But developing these tools has revealed some of the inherent challenges in trusting agentic AI to deliver 100% reliable chips.
“If you throw a spec at any kind of LLM or any kind of AI agent, it is bound to miss 20% to 30% of the intricacies of the spec,” Henry said. “It’s a very specific challenge within our industry, because building semiconductors is a zero-tolerance industry. If you have a bug, it’s a $10M problem because you can’t patch it or work around it. You have to rebuild the whole fleet of chips again. That’s why we spend so much time and effort on verification. That is the process we are trying to address and make really fast.”
That non-existent margin of error is also what makes the cross-disciplinary chip design expertise on Moores Lab AI’s staff so essential.
“It’s a very complex process and involves about 200 engineers. All these engineers have different specialties — design engineers, architects, verification engineers, DFT engineers, physical layout engineers, synthesis engineers,” he said. “We have to break down that problem into all these specialties and how we can build an AI system to accelerate these different specialties so that the final thing will compress. That has been our holy grail — how to get all these things working with AI.”
Henry said that one of the biggest challenges for his company going forward will be demonstrating results to engineering teams in a way that clearly cuts through the AI hype.
“It’s a challenging time for our customers, because there is a lot of noise in this space and they’re getting bombarded with all these offers,” Henry said. “Our new approach is to say, ‘Let us come in, take up one project, and show you what we can deliver. At the end of that project, it will match and exceed what your engineers have done for that exact project over the last nine years. Once we demonstrate that, then let’s talk about the next project.’ That’s been very well received.”
